article.title: The Capitulation Journal
article.description: Aditya Krishnan's (38, principal engineer, ₹3.1 Cr in equity) reluctant conversion from renter-evangelist to buyer — a written ₹3.4 Cr cap, an all-in cost said aloud at showflats, and a ₹3.8 Cr flat defeated by forty minutes of seasonal light.
article.quote: "I wrote the rent-vs-buy thread. Then I turned 38."

tabs.title: Who he is
tabs.description: Getting to know Aditya Krishnan (38, principal engineer, HSR's most articulate renter) — a decade-long rent-vs-buy evangelist converting at 38 after a polite eviction, a daughter's school, and a landlord who wanted 'no non-veg in the kitchen.'

buyers.name: Aditya Krishnan
buyers.description: For a decade he evangelized the spreadsheet gospel — renting + investing the difference beats buying, QED. The spreadsheet never broke; life did. Now buying anyway, on his terms: certainty priced as such, caps written down, and no marble-lobby lifestyle inflation.

chatMessages.text: Riya, the three-point-eight one. The light in that living room at four pm… I stood there and my cap — MY cap, which I wrote, laminated basically — started negotiating with me.

Then let's price the light. Forty lakhs above your cap, and the sun path says that specific light exists roughly forty minutes a day, October to February. You wrote the cap when you were rational precisely so it could out-vote you in nice light.

tabs.insightTitle: What I noticed while we were searching
tabs.insightDescription: “Aditya negotiates with his own psychology in writing — caps on tab one, wobbles priced in nouns, the concession thread drafted before the cheque. When the ₹3.8 Cr flat's better light started negotiating with his cap, we priced the sun: forty lakhs for forty minutes of seasonal light. The wobble died in the spreadsheet where it had always belonged. His real purchase wasn't a flat — it was control, school continuity, and walls he can drill without a WhatsApp negotiation. The yield cell was always silent about those.”

differentlyCards.title: Write the cap before the wobble exists
differentlyCards.description: The cap was written in month two — had it been written in month one, the ₹3.8 Cr visit might never have happened.

differentlyCards.title: Price the all-in from the first listing sheet
differentlyCards.description: The +31% decoder should have been a formula in the sheet from day one, not a habit acquired at showflat three.

differentlyCards.title: Ask for RWA financials in the first email
differentlyCards.description: Adding the request to the initial enquiry would have eliminated the non-disclosing finalist three weeks earlier.

differentlyCards.title: Draft the concession thread in month one
differentlyCards.description: The commitment device worked — but it would have worked even earlier, as the very first entry in the journal.

chatMessages.text: My old threads get quote-tweeted at me, and you know what? I'd buy again. The spreadsheet was right about money and silent about everything else.
That's the thread. And the forty-minute sun that cost forty lakhs will still be there in October — you just won't be paying for it.

tabs.adviceDescription: For buyers converting from rent-beats-buy orthodoxy, the edge is not in the model — it's in writing the cap down before the wobble exists, pricing the all-in cost aloud at every showflat, and drafting the public concession before the cheque. Aditya proved that a written cap is past-you doing present-you a favour, and that the old thesis can live inside the new one: a loan taken despite cash keeps ₹2 Cr+ compounding while certainty gets purchased at a known price.

checklistItems: You publicly argued rent-beats-buy for a decade, and life quietly changed your inputs.
A landlord's polite eviction taught you that control doesn't appear in yield calculations.
A child's school has become the fixed point your geography orbits.
You distinguish the financial asset from the consumption good, out loud, at parties.
